title: Efficient option pricing with unary-based photonic computing chip and generative adversarial learning
abstract_summary: The paper presents a photonic-chip implementation of a unary encoding approach for European option pricing that integrates generative adversarial networks for on-chip distribution loading and quantum amplitude estimation for quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo sampling. The unary photonic architecture simplifies circuit depth and uses local linear-optical operations, while on-chip GAN training captures market distributions; experimental demonstrations show improved convergence and feasibility for specialized financial photonic processors.
methodology_description: The authors implement a unary encoding-based option pricing pipeline on an integrated photonic chip. The methodology comprises three main modules: (1) distribution loading, (2) payoff calculation, and (3) iterative amplitude estimation for acceleration. Distribution loading is accomplished by encoding a discretized asset-price probability distribution into path-encoded single-photon amplitudes across n waveguides (unary basis). A variational photonic generator (parameterized by on-chip thermo-optic phase shifters) is embedded on-chip and trained as part of a hybrid Wasserstein GAN: the photonic generator produces fake samples (photon count probabilities across waveguides) while a classical neural-network discriminator (implemented in TensorFlow) evaluates them. The generator is optimized using a gradient-free evolutionary algorithm; the discriminator uses gradient-descent. After learning/loading the distribution via a linear-depth swap-network characterized by splitting parameters p (depth = floor((n+1)/2)), a controlled rotation network encodes payoff values into ancilla waveguides via pairwise Ry(θ) rotations (each unary bin is represented by two waveguides to avoid non-local controlled gates). Amplitude estimation is implemented without phase estimation by iteratively applying an amplitude-amplification operator Q = P·D·S0·D†·P†·Sψ (realized optically by phase shifts and reversing the earlier operations). Repeating Q m times (m up to 50 in experiments) amplifies the ancilla amplitude that encodes the expected payoff; measuring the ancilla |1⟩ population yields the expected payoff (rescaled by normalization). Experiments used single photons generated on-chip via degenerate SFWM and detected with SNSPDs; the GAN experiments used up to 8 bins while the full option-pricing demonstration used a 3-bin setup. Metrics reported include L2 distance between generated and target distributions, standard deviation and absolute error of payoff estimates, and empirical scaling demonstrating improved convergence from iterative amplitude amplification compared to classical Monte Carlo sampling.
algorithms_used: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (amplitude amplification without phase estimation)
experimental_setup: Integrated silicon photonic chip with reconfigurable thermo-optic phase shifters (each controlled by electronic current drivers, 1 kHz, 12-bit). Single-photon source: degenerate photon pairs generated via on-chip Spontaneous Four-Wave Mixing (SFWM) pumped by an Ultrafast Optical Clock (PriTel) at 500 MHz repetition rate, central wavelength 1550.116 nm, bandwidth 1.9 nm. Output photons filtered by WDM. Detectors: superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) from PhotonSpot (≈100 Hz dark counts, ≈85% efficiency). Polarization controllers before detectors. Time tagging using Swabian Instruments time tagger (≥40M events/s). Temperature controller for chip stability. Chip supports up to 8 unary bins for GAN experiments; the option-pricing experiment used a 3-bin (6-waveguide) configuration. GAN generator implemented as variational photonic circuit (phase shifters); classical discriminator implemented offline on CPU/GPU via TensorFlow. Measurements: single-photon counts per waveguide; in AE experiments 50 repeated measurements per step were reported.
dataset_used: Synthetic distributions: log-normal and normal target distributions were used as 'real' samples for GAN training. No explicit real-market dataset was reported for the experiments; the paper notes that market data would be the real-sample source in practical applications but experiments used synthetic distributions (log-normal/normal).

experiment_input.source: Synthetic samples drawn from target analytical distributions (log-normal and normal).
experiment_input.size: Not specified (GAN training referred to 100 training iterations and used per-iteration sampled photon-count distributions across up to 8 bins).
experiment_input.preprocessing: Continuous asset-price distributions were discretized/binned into n bins (unary basis). For the option-pricing demonstration, the 3-bin mapping was used (each bin represented by a pair of waveguides). Generator randomness leveraged photon-count uncertainty rather than an explicit classical noise vector.

pipeline_steps: 1) Prepare target distribution (synthetic log-normal or normal) and initialize photonic generator parameters.

2) GAN training loop: (a) Run photonic generator (variational circuit) to produce fake samples (photon probabilities across bins); (b) Feed fake and real samples to classical discriminator; (c) Update discriminator via gradient descent using Wasserstein objective; (d) Evaluate discriminator scores and update generator using evolutionary/gradient-free optimization (selection, crossover, mutation). Repeat (GAN experiments reported ~100 iterations).
3) After training, load learned distribution into unary photonic register via swap-based linear-depth circuit parameterized by p splitting parameters (depth = floor((n+1)/2)).
4) Apply payoff calculation module: pairwise Ry rotations between each bin's two waveguides to encode payoff amplitude (angles θi computed from asset price bin and strike normalization).

5) Perform iterative amplitude estimation: apply Sψ (phase flips on ancilla-encoding waveguides), apply P† and D†, apply S0 (phase flip on input waveguide), then D and P to form Q. Repeat Q m times (m varied from 0 to 50 in experiments).
6) Measure ancilla |1⟩ counts to estimate sin^2((2m+1)α) and infer expected payoff. Aggregate repeated measurements (50 repeats per step reported) to compute standard deviation and error.

[supported] Embedded a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) into the distribution-loading module and performed on-chip generator training with a classical discriminator in a hybrid scheme.

[supported] Showed experimentally that performing iterative amplitude amplification steps improves payoff-estimation accuracy and reduces estimation variance compared to a single (m=0) sampling run.

[supported] Designed the optical circuit so each unary basis element maps to a pair of waveguides (ancilla encoded as extra path), avoiding nonlocal controlled gates and enabling implementation in linear optics.

[supported] Used a hybrid GAN training approach: evolutionary (gradient-free) optimization for the on-chip generator parameters and gradient-based optimization for the classical discriminator, together with a Wasserstein training objective.

results_summary: The preprint reports a proof-of-principle implementation of a unary-option-pricing pipeline on a reconfigurable silicon photonic chip. The system integrates an on-chip variational generator (trained in a hybrid GAN loop with a classical discriminator) to load discrete asset-price distributions, a payoff-encoding stage that uses ancilla-path encoding, and an iterative amplitude-amplification procedure to improve measurement-based payoff estimates. Experimentally, the authors trained the generator to reproduce 8-bin synthetic target distributions (ℓ2 ≈ −18 dB), and for a 3-asset option instance showed that iterative amplitude amplification (up to m=50) reduced the standard deviation of payoff estimates from ~0.2 to <0.004 and improved estimation error relative to single-shot sampling. They argue (based on known amplitude estimation theory) that this unary+amplitude-estimation approach provides an asymptotic quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo sampling, and they claim practical advantages for photonic realizations due to simpler circuit connectivity and potential energy-efficiency benefits.
performance_claims: GAN ℓ2 convergence to target distributions: final ℓ2 ≈ −18 dB (8-bin generator trained, synthetic log-normal and normal targets).
Amplitude-estimation experimental run: standard deviation of payoff estimates reduced from ~0.2 (m=0) to <0.004 after iterative amplitude amplification (m up to 50).
Amplitude-amplification iterations performed experimentally up to m = 50 for the 3-asset proof-of-principle instance.
Reported (in comparison table) KL-divergence estimates: unary distribution-loading error ~10^-3 vs binary ~10^-2 (presented as comparative figures in Appendix D).
Reported (in comparison table) payoff deviation due to single-qubit error: unary ~25% vs binary ~35% (presented as comparative figures in Appendix D).
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors invoke known amplitude-estimation theory to claim an asymptotic quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo sampling for option pricing (O(1/m) vs O(1/sqrt(m))). Their small-scale photonic experiment demonstrates improved convergence/variance reduction in a 3-asset instance using iterative amplitude amplification, but it does not constitute a large-scale, practical demonstration of the quadratic advantage; therefore the advantage is presented as a theoretical/asymptotic claim supported by limited experimental evidence at small scale.
limitations: Proof-of-concept scale: the experimental photonic chip demonstration is limited to a small-instance problem (three asset values for the unary option-pricing experiment; up to eight bins used to demonstrate the GAN).
Circuit depth and implementation constraints: unitary matrices were multiplied and uploaded at constant depth to stay within depth limits of the fabricated device.

GAN training challenges stated by the authors: difficulty obtaining gradients from stochastic single-photon measurements and the discriminator easily overpowering the generator; required hybrid training (gradient-free evolutionary optimization for the generator and classical gradient descent for the discriminator) and use of Wasserstein distance.
Hardware noise and imperfections: chip crosstalk, losses and other imperfections affect operation and must be incorporated into on-chip training and/or mitigated.

Resource scaling trade-offs: unary encoding simplifies gate structure but requires a linear (in the number of bins) number of waveguides; achieving higher precision or larger state spaces therefore consumes more physical resources (waveguides, detectors).

Speedup vs resource cost: the reported polynomial/quadratic speedup is achieved at the cost of increased physical resources (the authors note the trade-off of polynomial speedups at the cost of exponential resources in related contexts).

Limited detector architecture in the demonstration: although the authors propose combining ancilla waveguide detectors into a single detector for scalability, the experimental work still uses multiple detectors and the multi-detector setup is a resource burden.
Use of single photons in the GAN introduces stochasticity that complicates training and sampling; alternatives such as coherent light are mentioned but involve trade-offs.
open_questions: Scalability: How to scale the photonic unary approach to practical, industry-relevant option-pricing instances with many more bins/assets while keeping resource usage and error rates manageable?

Noise and error robustness: To what extent does the quadratic speedup from amplitude estimation survive in the presence of realistic loss, detector inefficiency, thermal crosstalk, and other hardware noise?

Resource vs advantage trade-off: What is the precise trade-off between the physical-resource overhead (waveguides, detectors, heaters, control electronics) and the computational/energy advantage over classical Monte Carlo in realistic settings?

GAN on-chip training at scale: How well can on-chip GAN training generalize to high-dimensional, realistic market distributions (multivariate, time-dependent), and what are the limits imposed by sampling noise and measurement rates?

Amplitude estimation method: How does the iterative amplitude-estimation variant used (without phase estimation) compare, in practice and under noise, to other amplitude-estimation algorithms with respect to accuracy, resource requirements, and robustness?

Multi-photon / multi-mode generalization: How to extend the approach to multi-photon encodings or higher photon-number states to represent more complex distributions or correlation structures, and what are the practical challenges?

Detector consolidation feasibility: What are the practical implications, trade-offs, and technical difficulties of consolidating ancilla detections into a single detector as suggested for scalability?

Energy-efficiency quantification: What is the quantitative energy (and cost) advantage of the photonic implementation versus classical electronic alternatives when evaluated end-to-end for real workloads?

Integration into financial workflows: How to integrate such photonic processors into existing financial pipelines, including data ingestion, model updating, latency constraints, and regulatory/compliance requirements?

Comparison to classical alternatives: Beyond classical Monte Carlo, how does this unary photonic approach compare to state-of-the-art classical numerical/ML option-pricing methods in accuracy, runtime, and operational cost?
